title: Why the Dragon Hates God’s People
paragraphs:
Why the Dragon Hates God’s People
The Ancient War Most People Don’t Realize They’re Living In
Some battles are fought with swords.
Some with armies.
Some with words.
But there is another battle that has been raging since before your first breath—a war older than nations, older than empires, older than every kingdom that has risen and fallen from the dust.
Most people never see it.
They only feel the consequences.
The unexplained heaviness.
The temptation that appears at the worst possible moment.
The fear that whispers after midnight.
The shame that refuses to let go.
The constant resistance every time they try to move closer to God.
Scripture reveals that behind these struggles stands an ancient enemy represented as a dragon.
Not a mythical creature from folklore.
Not a symbolic villain invented by storytellers.
But a real spiritual adversary whose hatred burns with relentless fury against God and against everyone who bears His image.
The question is not whether the dragon exists.
The question is why he hates God's people so much.
To understand the answer, we must travel back to the beginning.
Back before Revelation.
Back before Rome.
Back before Israel.
Back before Bethlehem.
Back to a rebellion that changed everything.
The final book of Scripture pulls back the curtain and reveals what human eyes cannot naturally see.
Revelation 12:9 declares:
"And the great dragon was cast out, that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan, which deceiveth the whole world."
The Greek text calls him:
ὁ δράκων ὁ μέγας (ho drakōn ho megas)
"The great dragon."
This is not merely describing appearance.
The word δράκων (drakōn) was associated with a terrifying, destructive force—a predator that devours and destroys.
The dragon is identified as the serpent of Genesis, the devil, and Satan.
One enemy.
One rebellion.
One war.
His hatred began because he desired what belongs to God alone.
The prophet Isaiah records a rebellion often understood to describe the pride behind Satan's fall:
"I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High." (Isaiah 14:14)
The Hebrew phrase is:
אֶדַּמֶּה לְעֶלְיוֹן
(’eddammeh le‘elyon)
"I will make myself like the Most High."
Pride became treason.
Ambition became rebellion.
Rebellion became war.
And when Satan lost heaven, his hatred found a new target.
Humanity.
Why?
Because mankind possesses something Satan can never have again.
The favor of God.
The image of God.
The love of God.
Genesis tells us that humanity was created in the image of God:
בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים
(betselem Elohim)
"In the image of God."
Every human being carries divine significance.
Every person possesses immeasurable value.
Every soul reflects the craftsmanship of its Creator.
The dragon hates humanity because humanity reminds him of the God he tried to overthrow.
Every person becomes a living reminder of his defeat.
This explains why the enemy's attacks often focus on identity.
He attacks marriages.
Families.
Children.
Purity.
Purpose.
Truth.
Hope.
Anything that reflects God's design becomes a target.
But Revelation reveals an even deeper reason for his hatred.
The dragon particularly hates God's covenant people because through them came the Messiah.
Revelation 12 portrays a woman giving birth to a child destined to rule the nations.
The imagery points to God's redemptive plan culminating in Jesus Christ.
The dragon waits to devour the child.
Yet he fails.
Every attempt fails.
Pharaoh failed.
Herod failed.
The religious leaders failed.
Rome failed.
The grave failed.
Because God's plan cannot be stopped.
The dragon's hatred toward God's people is ultimately hatred toward Christ Himself.
This is why Jesus warned His followers:
"If the world hate you, ye know that it hated me before it hated you." (John 15:18)
The conflict is personal.
Not because believers are extraordinary.
But because they belong to Christ.
The dragon cannot strike the risen King.
So he attacks the King's people.
Yet this is where the story takes a breathtaking turn.
The dragon's greatest defeat came through what appeared to be his greatest victory.
At Calvary, darkness seemed to win.
The Son of God was beaten.
Mocked.
Humiliated.
Crucified.
The disciples scattered.
Hope appeared buried.
Hell celebrated too early.
Because the cross was never defeat.
It was divine strategy.
Colossians 2:15 tells us that Christ:
"disarmed the powers and authorities."
The Greek word is:
ἀπεκδυσάμενος
(apekdysamenos)
Meaning to strip away weapons and authority.
At the cross, Jesus exposed the enemy's powerlessness before God's sovereign plan.
What looked like scandal became salvation.
What looked like ruin became redemption.
What looked like the end became the beginning.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
And it is the reason the dragon continues to rage.
Revelation 12:12 explains:
"He knoweth that he hath but a short time."
The dragon is furious because he knows his future.
He knows the verdict has already been rendered.
He knows the cross sealed his doom.
He knows the empty tomb announced his defeat.
He knows King Jesus is returning.
His war against God's people is the rage of a defeated enemy.
Not a victorious one.
That truth changes everything.
Many believers spend years living as though they are fighting for victory.
Scripture teaches they are fighting from victory.
The outcome has already been decided through Christ.
This does not mean the battle is easy.
It means the battle is not uncertain.
The same chapter that describes the dragon's fury also describes the believers' triumph:
"And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony." (Revelation 12:11)
Notice what the verse does not say.
It does not say they overcame through talent.
Through influence.
Through wealth.
Through political power.
Through popularity.
They overcame through the blood of the Lamb.
The victory belongs to Jesus.
Always has.
Always will.
Perhaps that is why this ancient war feels so personal.
The dragon wants you to forget who you are.
He wants shame to speak louder than grace.
He wants fear to speak louder than faith.
He wants your failures to speak louder than the cross.
He wants your past to become your identity.
But Jesus specializes in rewriting stories.
The adulterer became forgiven.
The tax collector became transformed.
The persecutor became an apostle.
The thief became a testimony.
The scandal became grace.
The cross became a throne.
And sinners became sons and daughters of God.
Maybe as you read these words, you recognize the battle.
The temptation.
The exhaustion.
The disappointment.
The hidden wounds.
The prayers that seem unanswered.
The nights when faith feels fragile.
You are not imagining the war.
But neither should you forget who stands beside you in it.
The dragon may hate God's people.
But Christ loves them more than words can describe.
The same Savior who conquered death now intercedes for His people.
The same King who defeated the grave walks with His church.
The same Lamb who shed His blood still saves, restores, heals, and redeems.
This is why the Gospel remains the most powerful story ever told.
Not because it ignores scandal.
But because it transforms scandal into grace.
Not because it hides brokenness.
But because it redeems brokenness.
Not because it denies failure.
But because it rewrites failure through the mercy of Jesus Christ.
And perhaps that is exactly why the dragon hates God's people.
Because every redeemed life is evidence that he lost.
Every transformed heart is proof that Christ reigns.
Every testimony is a declaration that grace is stronger than sin.
Every believer is a living monument to the triumph of the cross.
The dragon knows it.
He fears it.
And he cannot stop it.
What battle has God been helping you overcome lately?
One day the dragon's voice will be silenced forever, but the scars transformed by Christ's grace will shine as eternal evidence that redemption had the final word.
